lesson.title: geben & give Family Tour
lesson.subtitle: geben/Gabe/vergeben radiation — with the Perfekt forms gab and gegeben

hook.title: One Root, a Dynasty
hook.content: geben is not one word — it is a dynasty. The verb geben (give) radiates: die Gabe (the gift — the verb frozen into a noun), vergeben (to forgive — literally to give completely away, the exact construction of for-give!), das Geschenk (the gift — a different root, the false-friend Gift is 'poison'!), es gibt (there is — literally 'it gives', the same impersonal trick as French il y a). And the ablaut forms you own: gab, gegeben. English runs the same dynasty from give: gift, forgive, given. Walk the family tree and every branch is a twin.

footnotes.title: Forgive and vergeben: the Same Coinage
footnotes.content: Both 'forgive' and 'vergeben' are 'give completely away' — for-/ver- intensifying the giving into release. Two languages coined the same metaphor independently... because they inherited the parts from the same toolbox. Even 'die Gabe' and 'gift' are the same ancient noun, which is exactly why German's Gift (poison) is the false-friend deck's star trap.

pattern.title: The Dynasty Walk
pattern.content: The verb: geben, gab, gegeben ↔ give, gave, given. The impersonal: es gibt ↔ there is ('it gives') — Es gibt ein Problem. The noun: die Gabe (the gift/talent — 'a giving'), with English gift as the twin. The prefix verb: vergeben, vergab, vergeben ↔ forgive, forgave, forgiven — ver-/for- + geben/give, the complete dynasty in one word. The feeling form: gefallen (it falls to me = it pleases me) — a different root but the same dative grammar: Es gefällt mir. Sentence plan: Ich habe ihm das Buch gegeben — geben, dative receiver, accusative thing, participle closing the bracket.
pattern.linguist_note: 'Es gibt' is the Germanic version of existence-as-giving: God gives, therefore there is. English kept the construction only in fossil phrases ('there's' was once 'there is' the same way). The Perfekt: es hat gegeben — though Germans prefer es gab for the past.

exercises.prompt: The dynasty — match each family member with its English twin:
exercises.target_answer: geben, vergeben, die Gabe, es gibt
exercises.meaning: to give, to forgive, the gift, there is
exercises.explanation: One root radiates through both languages: give, forgive, gift, 'it gives'.

exercises.prompt: 'Es gibt ein Problem' — what does 'gibt' literally mean here?
exercises.explanation: German says 'it gives a problem' where English says 'there is' — the impersonal-give construction.

exercises.prompt: Trap alert: which German word means a wrapped PRESENT, and which means POISON?
options: das Geschenk = present; das Gift = poison
das Gift = present; das Geschenk = poison
exercises.target_answer: das Geschenk = present; das Gift = poison
exercises.explanation: Both descend from 'a giving': English kept the friendly branch (gift), German kept the dose branch (poison). Say das Geschenk for presents.

exercises.explanation: haben → have and sieben → seven both showcase the V↔B consonant bridge (while Gabe and Gift show how roots diverge). [Ref: Wir haben es ihm gegeben]

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I have given him the book'
exercises.target_answer: Ich habe ihm das Buch gegeben
exercises.meaning: I have given him the book
exercises.explanation: The full dynasty in one bracket: geben's participle, the dative receiver ihm, the accusative thing — give gave given, to-him.

summary.outcome: Radiate geben into its noun, prefix-verbs, and Perfekt forms — and dodge the Gift trap.

use_example.german: Ich habe ihm das Buch gegeben.
use_example.english: I have given him the book.

summary.takeaway: geben is a dynasty: Gabe, vergeben/forgive, es gibt — and das Gift is poison, say Geschenk for presents.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the v→b word hunt — the whole quiet family, hunted through the Atlas bridge.

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

gefallen.context_translation: I like it (it falls well to me).
gefallen.etymology_derivation: ge- + fallen — 'to fall to someone' (by lot or liking), like English 'as it falls out'. Strong verb: gefiel, gefallen. [wiktionary]

mir.context_translation: Can you please help me? (literally: help to me)
mir.etymology_derivation: Dative of ich — the same ancient pronoun as English me, keeping the 'to me' meaning (mir ist kalt = it is cold to me). [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

rolle.etymology_derivation: Direct cognate from Latin rotula (little wheel / scroll of parchment for actors).

blitz.etymology_derivation: Old High German blëcchazzen — English bleak/bleach are the cognates; English blitz is a loan from German. [wiktionary]

kosten.context_translation: How much does the bread cost?
kosten.etymology_derivation: Latin loan via Old French coster, from Latin cōnstō — the same Romance source as English cost. [wiktionary]

kirsche.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic kirsija, an early borrowing of Late Latin ceresia; English cherry comes from the same Latin word, its ch being a later English palatalization. [wiktionary]

ehrlich.etymology_derivation: Ehre (honour) plus -lich, inherited from Middle High German erlich and Old High German erlih, built on the old honour root of Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys-. [wiktionary]

lippe.context_phrase: Sie beißt sich auf die Lippe.
lippe.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German and northern Middle High German lippe, from Old High German *lippa, from Proto-West Germanic *lippjō, the same form behind English lip. [wiktionary]

apotheker.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German apotēker, from Latin apothecarius (storekeeper) - the very word that became English apothecary. [wiktionary][etymonline]

übermorgen.context_translation: The day after tomorrow I am going to Berlin.
übermorgen.etymology_derivation: über + morgen — the exact structural twin of the archaic English adverb overmorrow, which Wiktionary records as a calque of this German word. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
